{{Short description|Partition of the Euclidean plane}}
[[File:Power diagram.svg|thumb|300px|A power diagram of four circles]]
In [[computational geometry]], a '''power diagram''', also called a '''Laguerre–Voronoi diagram''', '''Dirichlet cell complex''', '''radical Voronoi tesselation''' or a '''sectional Dirichlet tesselation''', is a partition of the [[Euclidean plane]] into [[polygon]]al cells defined from a set of circles. The cell for a given circle ''C'' consists of all the points for which the [[Power of a point|power distance]] to ''C'' is smaller than the power distance to the other circles. The power diagram is a form of generalized [[Voronoi diagram]], and coincides with the Voronoi diagram of the circle centers in the case that all the circles have equal radii.<ref>{{citation

 }}.</ref><ref name="iim85">{{citation

==Definition==
[[File:Valor de la potencia de un punto - caso exterior.svg|thumb|The power of a point ''P'' outside of a given circle]]
If ''C'' is a circle and ''P'' is a point outside ''C'', then the [[Power of a point|power]] of ''P'' with respect to ''C'' is the square of the length of a [[line segment]] from ''P'' to a point ''T'' of tangency with ''C''. Equivalently, if ''P'' has distance ''d'' from the center of the circle, and the circle has radius ''r'', then (by the [[Pythagorean theorem]]) the power is ''d''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''r''<sup>2</sup>. The same formula ''d''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''r''<sup>2</sup> may be extended to all points in the plane, regardless of whether they are inside or outside of ''C'': points on ''C'' have zero power, and points inside ''C'' have negative power.<ref name="iim85"/><ref name="a87"/><ref name="e87"/>

The power diagram of a set of ''n'' circles ''C''<sub>''i''</sub> is a partition of the plane into ''n'' regions ''R''<sub>''i''</sub> (called cells), such that a point ''P'' belongs to ''R''<sub>''i''</sub> whenever circle ''C''<sub>''i''</sub> is the circle minimizing the power of ''P''.<ref name="iim85"/><ref name="a87"/><ref name="e87"/>

[[File:Radical axis intersecting circles.svg|thumb|The radical axis of two intersecting circles. The power diagram of the two circles is the partition of the plane into two halfplanes formed by this line.]]
In the case ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, the power diagram consists of two [[halfplane]]s, separated by a line called the [[radical axis]] or chordale of the two circles. Along the radical axis, both circles have equal power. More generally, in any power diagram, each cell ''R''<sub>''i''</sub> is a [[convex polygon]], the intersection of the halfspaces bounded by the radical axes of circle ''C''<sub>''i''</sub> with each other circle. Triples of cells meet at [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]] of the diagram, which are the radical centers of the three circles whose cells meet at the vertex.<ref name="iim85"/><ref name="a87"/><ref name="e87"/>

==Related constructions==
The power diagram may be seen as a weighted form of the [[Voronoi diagram]] of a set of point sites, a partition of the plane into cells within which one of the sites is closer than all the other sites. Other forms of [[weighted Voronoi diagram]] include the additively weighted Voronoi diagram, in which each site has a weight that is added to its distance before comparing it to the distances to the other sites, and the multiplicatively weighted Voronoi diagram, in which the weight of a site is multiplied by its distance before comparing it to the distances to the other sites. In contrast, in the power diagram, we may view each circle center as a site, and each circle's squared radius as a weight that is subtracted from the [[squared Euclidean distance]] before comparing it to other squared distances. In the case that all the circle radii are equal, this [[subtraction]] makes no difference to the comparison, and the power diagram coincides with the Voronoi diagram.<ref name="a87"/><ref name="e87"/>

A planar power diagram may also be interpreted as a planar cross-section of an unweighted three-dimensional Voronoi diagram. In this interpretation, the set of circle centers in the cross-section plane are the perpendicular projections of the three-dimensional Voronoi sites, and the squared radius of each circle is a constant ''K'' minus the squared distance of the corresponding site from the cross-section plane, where ''K'' is chosen large enough to make all these radii positive.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ash | first1 = Peter F.
 | last2 = Bolker | first2 = Ethan D.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF00164401 | doi-access=
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Geometriae Dedicata]]
 | mr = 833848
 | pages = 209–243
 | title = Generalized Dirichlet tessellations
 | volume = 20
 | year = 1986| s2cid = 120383767
 }}.</ref>

Like the Voronoi diagram, the power diagram may be generalized to Euclidean spaces of any dimension. The power diagram of ''n'' spheres in ''d'' dimensions is combinatorially equivalent to the intersection of a set of ''n'' upward-facing halfspaces in ''d''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 dimensions, and vice versa.<ref name="a87"/>

==Algorithms and applications==
Two-dimensional power diagrams may be constructed by an algorithm that runs in time O(''n''&nbsp;log&nbsp;''n'').<ref name="iim85"/><ref name="a87"/> More generally, because of the equivalence with higher-dimensional halfspace intersections, ''d''-dimensional power diagrams (for ''d''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2) may be constructed by an algorithm that runs in time <math>O(n^{\lceil d/2\rceil})</math>.<ref name="a87"/>

The power diagram may be used as part of an efficient algorithm for computing the volume of a union of spheres. Intersecting each sphere with its power diagram cell gives its contribution to the total union, from which the volume may be computed in time proportional to the complexity of the power diagram.<ref name="abi88">{{citation
 | last1 = Avis | first1 = David | author1-link = David Avis
 | last2 = Bhattacharya | first2 = Binay K.
 | last3 = Imai | first3 = Hiroshi
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01901190 | doi-access=free
 | issue = 6
 | journal = The Visual Computer
 | pages = 323–328
 | title = Computing the volume of the union of spheres
 | url = http://cgm.cs.mcgill.ca/~avis/doc/avis/ABI88a.pdf
 | volume = 3
 | year = 1988}}.</ref>

Other applications of power diagrams include [[data structure]]s for testing whether a point belongs to a union of disks,<ref name="iim85"/> algorithms for constructing the boundary of a union of disks,<ref name="iim85"/> and algorithms for finding the closest two balls in a set of balls.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Guibas | first1 = Leonidas | author1-link = Leonidas J. Guibas
 | last2 = Zhang | first2 = Li
 | contribution = Euclidean proximity and power diagrams
 | title = 10th Canadian Conference on Computational Geometry
 | url = http://www.cccg.ca/proceedings/1998/cccg98-guibas-euclidean.ps.gz
 | year = 1998}}.</ref> It is also used for solving the semi-discrete [[Transportation theory (mathematics)|optimal transportation]] problem<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aurenhammer |first1=F. |last2=Hoffmann |first2=F. |last3=Aronov |first3=B. |date=January 1998 |title=Minkowski-Type Theorems and Least-Squares Clustering |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/PL00009187 |journal=Algorithmica |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=61–76 |doi=10.1007/PL00009187 |s2cid=5409198 |issn=0178-4617|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which in turn has numerous applications, such as early universe reconstruction<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Levy |first1=Bruno |last2=Mohayaee |first2=Roya |last3=von Hausegger |first3=Sebastian |date=2021-07-13 |title=A fast semidiscrete optimal transport algorithm for a unique reconstruction of the early Universe |url=https://academic.oup.com/mnras/article/506/1/1165/6300452 |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |language=en |volume=506 |issue=1 |pages=1165–1185 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stab1676 |doi-access=free |issn=0035-8711|arxiv=2012.09074 }}</ref> or [[fluid dynamics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lévy |first=Bruno |date=February 2022 |title=Partial optimal transport for a constant-volume Lagrangian mesh with free boundaries |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021999121007336 |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |language=en |volume=451 |article-number=110838 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2021.110838|arxiv=2106.03936 |bibcode=2022JCoPh.45110838L |s2cid=235406800 }}</ref>

==History==
{{harvtxt|Aurenhammer|1987}} traces the definition of the power distance to the work of 19th-century mathematicians [[Edmond Laguerre]] and [[Georgy Voronoy]].<ref name="a87"/> {{harvtxt|Fejes Tóth|1977}} defined power diagrams and used them to show that the boundary of a union of ''n'' circular disks can always be illuminated from at most 2''n'' point light sources.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Fejes Tóth | first = L. | author-link = László Fejes Tóth
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01895856 | doi-access=
 | issue = 3–4
 | journal = [[Acta Mathematica Hungarica|Acta Mathematica Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae]]
 | mr = 0464065
 | pages = 355–360
 | title = Illumination of convex discs
 | volume = 29
 | year = 1977| s2cid = 122510545 }}.</ref> Power diagrams have appeared in the literature under other names including the "Laguerre–Voronoi diagram", "Dirichlet cell complex", "radical Voronoi tesselation" and "sectional Dirichlet tesselation".<ref name="ai88">{{citation
 | last1 = Aurenhammer | first1 = F.
 | last2 = Imai | first2 = H.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF00181613 | doi-access=
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Geometriae Dedicata]]
 | mr = 950323
 | pages = 65–75
 | title = Geometric relations among Voronoĭ diagrams
 | volume = 27
 | year = 1988}}.</ref>
